sections.text: Ninety-nine trials test CD20-targeting drugs in multiple sclerosis (MS), with 47 in Phase 3 and 23 in Phase 4.
Roche leads with 35 trials, followed by Novartis with 16 and TG Therapeutics with 9.
Three CD20-targeting drugs—ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, and ublituximab—are approved for relapsing forms of MS.
Multiple trials have stopped: one due to business reasons, one due to slow enrollment, one due to funding loss, and another due to geopolitical conflict.
A 2026 pharmacovigilance study found signals of non-PML neuroinvasive infections with anti-CD20 therapies in MS.
A 2026 perspective highlights uncertainty around anti-CD20 discontinuation, noting disease reactivation after cessation and lack of predictive biomarkers.
A 2026 cohort study in JAMA Neurology reported an increased risk of inflammatory bowel disease following anti-CD20 treatment in MS.
The median stop-risk for CD20 trials in MS is 0.249, based on the site's risk model.
FDA labels for ocrelizumab and ofatumumab include warnings for infections, infusion/injection reactions, immunoglobulin reduction, and malignancy risk.

read: Mechanism evidence: CD20 inhibition is well-established in MS with multiple approved agents and extensive trial activity, but carries risks of infection, IBD, and neuroinvasive events.
Competitive position: Dominated by major players and three approved drugs, but discontinuation uncertainty and safety signals may limit long-term use.
Open questions: Can lower stop-risk strategies be developed? Are biomarkers for safe discontinuation feasible?
would_change: Evidence of safe and predictable treatment discontinuation would favor investment.
Demonstration of reduced infection or IBD risk compared to current anti-CD20 agents would shift the stance to favorable.
A significant drop in trial stop-risk below 0.2 would improve competitive outlook.
